Chapter 5

Special Provisions for People with Disabilities

The Dutch rules for disability parking cards, the specific parking exemptions in RVV Article 85, and recognition of cards issued outside the Netherlands.

  • RVV Article 85 — Parking Exemptions
  • RVV Article 86 — Foreign Cards

Chapter 5 of the RVV 1990 contains special provisions for people with disabilities. The central rule is Article 85, which gives a valid disability parking card (gehandicaptenparkeerkaart) a limited set of exemptions from specific parking rules. These exemptions are precise: the card does not create a general right to ignore all parking or no-stopping rules.

Article 86 deals with disability parking cards issued outside the Netherlands. The ministerial Regeling gehandicaptenparkeerkaart determines which foreign cards are treated as equivalent to a Dutch card.

§ 1 — Parking Exemptions Under Article 85

Know exactly which rules are set aside, when the three-hour limit applies, and which prohibitions still remain in force.

The Disability Parking Card Gehandicaptenparkeerkaart

The Dutch disability parking card is the European-style blue parking card with the wheelchair symbol. For an individual card, there are separate driver and passenger cards; there is also an institution card for the transport of residents of care institutions.

Individual cards are person-bound, not tied to one registration number. The legal parking benefits apply only when the parking is directly connected with transporting the person with a disability. An institution card is used for the transport of eligible residents of that institution.

♿
Article 85 — The Core Exemptions

For the driver of a motor vehicle with more than two wheels in which a valid and properly legible disability parking card is displayed, Article 85 provides the following exemptions when the parking is directly related to transporting a person with a disability:

  • Parking-disc zones — Article 25: Article 25 does not apply.
  • Yellow broken line — Article 24(1)(e): parking is allowed for no more than three hours.
  • Within an erf — Article 46: a motor vehicle may park outside the places specifically marked or designated for parking for no more than three hours.
  • No-parking sign E1 — Article 62: the E1 parking prohibition does not apply for no more than three hours.

In each of the three-hour situations, the vehicle must also have a clearly visible parking disc showing the time at which parking began.

What the Card Allows — and What It Does Not

General disabled parking spaces (E6)

A vehicle with a valid disability parking card may use a general disabled parking space when the parking is directly connected with transporting the person to whom the card was issued. A space reserved for a specific registration number remains reserved for that vehicle.

Parking-disc zones

Article 85 exempts the qualifying vehicle from the normal Article 25 parking-disc-zone rules. Other parking restrictions and any applicable local parking rules can still matter.

Yellow broken line

A yellow broken line normally means parking is prohibited. With the Article 85 exemption, a qualifying vehicle may park there for up to three hours, with a clearly visible parking disc.

No-parking sign E1

A qualifying vehicle may park for up to three hours where sign E1 (no parking) applies. A parking disc is required. This exemption does not extend to sign E2 (no stopping).

Parking within an erf

Article 46 normally requires motor vehicles in an erf to park only in marked or designated parking places. Article 85 allows a qualifying motor vehicle to park elsewhere within the erf for up to three hours, with a parking disc.

Paid parking is a local matter

The national disability parking card does not itself guarantee free parking in every municipality. Some municipalities offer free parking or special arrangements; others require payment or registration. Always check local rules.

Important — The Card Is Not a General Parking Exemption

Article 85 sets aside only the specific rules named above. It does not exempt the driver from the general no-stopping rules in Article 23, such as stopping on a crossing or within five metres of it, in a tunnel, in the prohibited area of a bus stop, on a cycle lane or the carriageway alongside it where Article 23 applies, or along a solid yellow line.

It also does not remove other parking prohibitions in Article 24, such as parking within five metres of an intersection, in front of an entrance or exit, or on the carriageway of a priority road outside a built-up area. In particular, a disability parking card does not exempt the driver from the priority-road carriageway prohibition in Article 24(1)(c).

Display the Card Correctly Front side visible

The card must be placed by the windscreen so that its front side can be properly read from outside the vehicle. Under the ministerial regulation, the “front” is the side showing the card’s expiry date.

A card that is expired, illegible or not displayed in the prescribed way does not satisfy the conditions for the Article 85 exemption.

The Three-Hour Rule Parking disc required

The three-hour limit is not a general rule for every use of a disability parking card. Under Article 85 it applies specifically to the exemptions for the yellow broken line, parking outside designated spaces within an erf, and sign E1.

When one of these three-hour exemptions is used, a clearly visible parking disc must show the time at which parking began.

A disabled parking space itself can also have a maximum parking duration shown on a supplementary plate. In that case the parking-disc rules stated for that space apply.
Driver Card, Passenger Card and Institution Card Different card types

A Dutch individual card can be issued as a driver card (B), a passenger card (P), or in qualifying cases a combined card. There is also an institution card (I) for the transport of residents of a care institution.

The key traffic-law principle is that use of the parking exemption must be directly connected with the transport of the person with a disability. An individual card is not a transferable parking permit for relatives or friends to use for unrelated parking.

Separate Rule — Certain Special Mopeds

Do not confuse the Article 85 parking exemptions with a separate rule in RVV Article 5. Drivers of certain bijzondere bromfietsen in the statutory category referred to there may use the pavement or footpath when they hold a disability parking card or another designated card. This is a place-on-the-road rule for that specific vehicle category, not a general privilege for every snorfiets and not part of the Article 85 parking exemption.

§ 2 — Disability Parking Cards Issued Outside the Netherlands

Article 86 refers foreign cards to the ministerial regulation that determines which cards are treated as equivalent to a Dutch disability parking card.

EU and EEA Cards Standard model

A disability parking card issued in another EU member state in the common European model is treated as equivalent to a Dutch card. The same rule expressly covers cards issued in another state that is party to the European Economic Area (EEA), such as Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Once a foreign card is legally treated as equivalent, the Dutch parking rules and limits apply while it is being used in the Netherlands.

Other Foreign Cards Wheelchair symbol test

The rule for cards from outside the EU/EEA is broader than a simple “treaty-country only” test. Under Article 6 of the Regeling gehandicaptenparkeerkaart, a card issued by a competent authority outside the Netherlands is also treated as equivalent if the front of the card carries the prescribed wheelchair symbol, or a symbol that is almost identical to it.

This means recognition of a non-EU card is not limited to countries that have a specific treaty with the Netherlands.

Recognition in the Netherlands
  • EU card in the common European model
  • EEA card in the common model
  • Other foreign card issued by a competent authority if the front carries the prescribed wheelchair symbol or a nearly identical symbol
Dutch use conditions still matter
  • The card must be valid and properly legible
  • It must be displayed in the prescribed way by the windscreen
  • The parking must be directly connected with transporting the person with a disability
  • Three-hour exemptions require a parking disc
  • Local paid-parking rules may still differ by municipality
If You Are Unsure About a Foreign Card Practical check

If the design or status of a foreign card is unclear, check before parking. The key Dutch legal question is whether the card falls within Article 6 of the Regeling gehandicaptenparkeerkaart. Municipal parking conditions can also matter, especially for paid parking.

Same Legal Exemptions — Same Limits

A foreign card that is treated as equivalent under Article 86 and the ministerial regulation receives the same Article 85 treatment as a Dutch disability parking card. That includes the same limited exemptions and the same three-hour parking-disc requirements. It does not create additional rights beyond those available to a Dutch card holder.

Chapter 5 — What to Take Away

Article 85 is precise. A qualifying motor vehicle displaying a valid disability parking card is exempt from Article 25, and for up to three hours from the yellow-broken-line rule in Article 24(1)(e), the parking restriction within an erf in Article 46, and sign E1 through Article 62. The three-hour cases require a clearly visible parking disc.

The card does not override general no-stopping rules or every other parking prohibition. Parking on the carriageway of a priority road outside a built-up area, for example, is not one of the Article 85 exemptions.

Article 86: foreign cards designated by the ministerial regulation are treated as equivalent. EU/EEA common-model cards qualify, and other foreign cards can also qualify when the front carries the prescribed wheelchair symbol or a nearly identical symbol.
